exam_guide_revision: Not a certification. Practical Python 3.10-3.14 fluency track; Domain 2 collections, built-ins, mappings, strings, and sets revalidated against official Python 3.14 documentation on 2026-09-22.

learning_design.unlock_rule: A knowledge node unlocks after all required prompts are completed, including required code or table discoveries.
learning_design.mastery_note: Discovery progress is not mastery evidence; progressively harder retrieval and typed coding questions provide the scored signal.

authoring_notes: Domain 2 quality pass: every knowledge node now combines short ADHD-friendly progressive explanations with the existing annotated code example. Each code example has one high-value click-to-reveal runtime result so the learner connects syntax with behavior. Progressive text hides one key phrase normally and at most two. Glossary terms are scoped per node and explain only supporting vocabulary. Facts were revalidated against official Python 3.14 documentation while preserving the track's Python 3.10-3.14 scope.

prompts.label: WHAT HAPPENS ON A MISSING KEY?

reveal.text: `defaultdict` can call a factory to create, insert, and return a value for a missing key.

reveal.code:
from collections import defaultdict

groups = defaultdict(list)

for name, team in [("Ada", "red"), ("Linus", "blue"), ("Grace", "red")]:
    groups[team].append(name)

annotations.title: Missing-value factory
annotations.explanation: list is called for a missing key, producing a fresh empty list.

annotations.title: Group without a manual existence check
annotations.explanation: The missing list is created when needed, then the name is appended.

prompts.label: PASS THE FACTORY, NOT ITS RESULT

reveal.text: Use `defaultdict(list)`, not `defaultdict(list())`: the constructor needs a callable it can invoke later.

prompts.label: GET() DOES NOT TRIGGER THE FACTORY

reveal.text: `mapping[key]` can invoke the missing-key factory; `mapping.get(key)` uses normal `dict.get()` behavior instead.

glossary.definition: A callable used to create a value when one is needed.
An object that can be called with parentheses, such as a function, method, or class.
A key that is not currently present in a mapping.

reveal.text: `Counter` maps each hashable value to its frequency count.

reveal.code:
from collections import Counter

events = ["ok", "error", "ok", "warn", "error", "ok"]
counts = Counter(events)
top_two = counts.most_common(2)

annotations.title: Get the top two
annotations.explanation: most_common returns the highest-frequency (value, count) pairs.

reveal.text: Reading a missing `Counter` key returns zero instead of raising `KeyError`.
`most_common()` orders equal-count ties by when elements were first encountered.

glossary.definition: Able to provide a stable hash value, which is required for dictionary keys and set members.
How many times a value occurs.
A situation where two or more values have the same comparison value or count.

prompts.label: WHY USE DEQUE FOR A FIFO QUEUE?

reveal.text: Appending on the right and removing with `popleft()` implements FIFO queue behavior.

reveal.code:
from collections import deque

queue = deque()
queue.append("job-1")
queue.append("job-2")
first = queue.popleft()

annotations.title: Enqueue right
annotations.explanation: append adds new work to the right side.

annotations.title: Dequeue left
annotations.explanation: popleft removes the oldest queued item efficiently.

prompts.label: FRONT REMOVAL IS THE KEY ADVANTAGE

reveal.text: `deque.popleft()` is approximately O(1), while repeated `list.pop(0)` requires O(n) movement.
`popleft()` on an empty deque raises `IndexError`, so guard or handle the empty case.

glossary.definition: First in, first out: the oldest queued item is processed first.
A collection where items wait to be processed in an intended order.
Constant-time growth behavior: the operation's cost stays roughly independent of collection size.
Linear-time growth behavior: the operation's cost grows roughly with the number of items.

reveal.text: `dict.setdefault(key, default)` returns the existing value, or inserts and returns `default` when the key is missing.

annotations.title: Get or create a group
annotations.explanation: If team is absent, setdefault stores the empty list; otherwise it returns the existing list.

prompts.label: WHY DOES THE GROUPING IDIOM WORK?

reveal.text: The returned list is the stored list, so `.append()` mutates the dictionary's group directly.

prompts.label: THE DEFAULT EXPRESSION IS EVALUATED FIRST

reveal.text: A default expression is evaluated before `setdefault()` runs, even when the key already exists.

glossary.definition: The expression used to produce the fallback value passed to a function or method.

reveal.text: `min()` and `max()` use the key function for comparison but return the original selected item.

reveal.code:
users = []

youngest = min(
    users,
    key=lambda user: user["age"],
    default=None,
)

annotations.title: Comparison key
annotations.explanation: min compares derived ages while returning the original user.

annotations.title: Empty-input fallback
annotations.explanation: default avoids ValueError when users is empty.

reveal.text: With the single-iterable form, `default=` supplies a fallback instead of raising `ValueError` on empty input.
If multiple items share the minimum or maximum key, Python returns the first encountered item.

glossary.definition: A function passed with `key=` that computes the value used for comparison.
A value returned when the normal result is unavailable.
A situation where two or more values have the same comparison value or count.

prompts.label: WHEN DO ANY() AND ALL() STOP?

reveal.text: `any()` short-circuits on the first truthy value; `all()` short-circuits on the first falsy value.

reveal.code:
values = [2, 4, 7, 10]

has_odd = any(value % 2 for value in values)
all_positive = all(value > 0 for value in values)

annotations.title: Stop at the first truthy item
annotations.explanation: any returns True as soon as one generated value is truthy.

annotations.title: Stop at the first false item
annotations.explanation: all returns False as soon as one generated value is false.

reveal.text: `any([])` is `False`, while `all([])` is `True`.
A generator expression lets `any()` or `all()` consume values lazily without building a temporary list.

glossary.definition: Stop evaluating as soon as the final result is already known.
A value treated as true in a Boolean context.
A value treated as false in a Boolean context.
A compact expression such as `(x for x in items)` that produces values lazily.

reveal.text: `dict.get(key, default)` returns the stored value or a fallback without raising `KeyError`.

prompts.label: READ WITH A FALLBACK
prompts.placeholder: Click get on the missing key.

annotations.title: Missing-key fallback
annotations.explanation: Because port is absent, get returns 5432 without inserting it into config.

prompts.label: GET() DOES NOT INSERT THE DEFAULT

reveal.text: Returning the fallback does not insert the missing key into the dictionary.
If you omit the second argument, a missing key makes `get()` return `None`.

glossary.definition: A value returned when the normal result is unavailable.
The exception raised by normal dictionary indexing when a key is missing.
Add a new key-value pair to a dictionary.

reveal.text: `str.partition(separator)` always returns a 3-tuple: text before, the separator, and text after the first match.

prompts.label: SPLIT ONCE AND KEEP THE SEPARATOR

reveal.code:
header = "Content-Type: application/json"

name, separator, value = header.partition(":")
value = value.strip()

annotations.title: Three-part split
annotations.explanation: partition returns (before, separator, after) using the first match.

reveal.text: If the separator is not found, `partition()` returns the original string followed by two empty strings.
Calling `partition("")` raises `ValueError`; the separator must contain at least one character.

glossary.definition: The delimiter string used to split text.
A tuple containing exactly three values.

reveal.text: `removeprefix()` and `removesuffix()` remove one exact prefix or suffix only when it appears at the matching edge.

annotations.title: Remove one exact prefix
annotations.explanation: The prefix is removed only when it appears at the start.

annotations.title: Remove one exact suffix
annotations.explanation: The suffix is removed only when it appears at the end.

reveal.text: If the exact affix is absent, these methods return an unchanged copy of the string.

prompts.label: DO NOT REPLACE THEM WITH LSTRIP/RSTRIP

reveal.text: `lstrip(chars)` and `rstrip(chars)` treat `chars` as a character set, not one exact prefix or suffix.

glossary.definition: Text expected at the beginning of a string.
Text expected at the end of a string.
A collection of individual characters rather than one exact substring.

prompts.label: READ SET OPERATORS AS MEMBERSHIP RELATIONSHIPS

reveal.text: `A & B` is intersection, `A - B` is left-side difference, and `A ^ B` is symmetric difference.

annotations.title: Difference
annotations.explanation: Members in expected but not received.

annotations.title: Reverse difference
annotations.explanation: Members received that were not expected.

reveal.text: `A - B` keeps members from `A` that are not in `B`; reversing the operands changes the result.

prompts.label: OPERATORS AND METHODS ACCEPT DIFFERENT INPUTS

reveal.text: Set operators such as `&` require set operands, while methods such as `.intersection()` accept any iterable.

glossary.definition: The members shared by both sets.
The members in the left set that are not in the right set.
The members that occur in exactly one of two sets.
